title: Career technical education experts to visit Maryland school districts
summary: Expert review teams focused on career and technical education will visit all 24 school districts under a two-year plan to find ways school officials can better partner with businesses and nonprofits to boost high school apprenticeship programs.
content:
by William J. Ford, Maryland Matters October 28, 2024

by William J. Ford, Maryland Matters October 28, 2024

Expert review teams focused on career and technical education have begun to visit all 24 school districts, the start of a two-year plan to help school officials find ways to partner with local businesses and nonprofit organizations to boost high school apprenticeship programs.

Under the plan, approved Thursday by the Blueprint for Maryland’s Future Accountability and Implementation Board (AIB), 26 schools in 13 school districts will be visited this school year by individuals who include members of the state’s Career and Technical Education Committee (CTE), staff with the state Department of Education and staff with local workforce development boards.

The plan calls for the committee to visit six school districts this fall and seven in the spring, with two schools visited in each district. During the 2025-26 school year, the teams will visit at least another nine school districts: five districts in the fall and four school districts in the spring of 2026.

Two Queen Anne’s County high schools and a CTE center in Anne Arundel County were visited last spring under a pilot program and will be revisited next school year “if time and resources allow,” according to the visit deployment plan approved by the AIB. It notes that schools to be visited will be chosen based on geography, academic performance and the level CTE of enrollment and completion, among other factors.

A focus on college and career readiness is one of the main priorities of the 10-year Blueprint for Maryland’s Future, the state’s sweeping education reform plan. Part of the CTE Committee’s responsibility will be working with department staff to collect data and assess apprenticeship programs.

“The follow up of what comes up next after the visits is still being developed,” said AIB Executive Director Rachel Hise. She said the review needs to look “not just in this area, but really defining what CTE pathways really look like and how we monitor progress.”

The board also approved an Apprenticeships for High School Students in Maryland policy that will require the committee to develop a plan to engage employers, organize regular meetings with state agencies and “consider equity challenges in apprenticeship expansion and what support, guidance and assistance might be needed for more rural communities with fewer employers.”

The Blueprint calls for at least 45% of high school students to complete a high-school level registered apprenticeship program or industry-recognized credential by the 2030-31 school year. The committee defines an industry-recognized credential as skills or competencies that align with state or regional workforce occupations within “in-demand fields,” such as information technology, business management and finance and health and biosciences.

In 2023, according to documents submitted to the board in September by the CTE committee, about 4,000 high school students obtained an industry-recognized credential or a little less than 7% of the 60,000 public school students the state graduates in a typical year.

A legislative work group called the Apprenticeship 2030 Commission is also tasked to provide recommendations to implement, assess and improve apprenticeship programs. The group, which includes state lawmakers, agency and education officials and business leaders, is scheduled to meet virtually Dec. 5.
